question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x)+8 x=0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=- 8 x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(- 8 x\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ f(x) &=-8\int x\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=-8\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)+C \\ &=- 4 x^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Solve the differential equation $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}- 8 e^{2 x}=8 x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} &=8 e^{2 x}+8 x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(8 e^{2 x}+8 x\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ y &=8\int e^{2 x}\,\mathrm{d}x+8\int x\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=8\left(\frac{e^{2 x}}{2}\right)+8\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)+C \\ &=4 x^{2} + 4 e^{2 x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Solve the differential equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=-7.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int -7\,\text{d}x \\  & =-7\int 1\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-7\left(x\right)+C \\  & =C - 7 x.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \left(C - 7 x\right)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =-7\int x\,\text{d}x+C\int \text{d}x \\  & =-7\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)+Cx+D \\  & =C x + D - \frac{7 x^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

knowledge_point.title: Solving an Inhibited Growth Model

question.:question/problem:
The number of students affected by flu $P(t)$ increases toward a maximum of $1500$ students. Time $t\ge 0$ is measured in days from the start of monitoring. At $t=0$, the quantity is $300$ students. At $t=10$, it is $500$ students. At what time $t$, measured from the start of monitoring, does the quantity reach $800$ students? Round to the nearest integer.

*Hint: Assume an inhibited growth model.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
The growth rate is proportional to the remaining deficit. Thus

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(1500-P).
$$

Separate and integrate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{1500-P}&=k\,dt \\ -\ln|1500-P|&=kt+C.\end{aligned}
$$

The deficit is positive on this growth branch. Exponentiating and setting $K=e^{-C}>0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1500-P&=e^{-kt-C} \\ &=Ke^{-kt} \\ P(t)&=1500-Ke^{-kt}.\end{aligned}
$$

Use the initial condition:

$$
K=1500-300=1200.
$$

Calibrate the rate with the later observation:

$$
\begin{aligned}1200e^{-10k}&=1000 \\ -10k&=\ln\left(\frac{5}{6}\right) \\ k&=\frac{1}{10}\ln\left(\frac{6}{5}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore

$$
P(t)=1500-1200e^{-kt}.
$$

For the requested target, solve for the original time $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}700&=1200e^{-k(t-0)} \\ -k(t-0)&=\ln\left(\frac{7}{12}\right) \\ t&=0+\frac{\ln\left(\frac{12}{7}\right)}{k} \\ &\approx 29.562961 \\ &\approx 30.\end{aligned}
$$

This is approximately $30$ days from the start of monitoring.
